concepts.title: Definition of Texture
concepts.one_liner: A texture is an image composed of similar-looking elements where the representation focuses on the statistics of the constituents rather than individual elements.
concepts.content: A texture is a type of image that is composed by a set of similar looking elements. A texture representation contains information about the statistics of its constituent elements, but not about the elements individually. This concept is intimately related to human perception.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining texture statistically allows us to describe complex surfaces (like grass or sand) without needing to model every individual blade or grain.
concepts.recap_md:
- Composed of a set of similar-looking constituent elements.
 - Defined by the statistics of elements rather than their individual identities.

 - Defined by the statistics of elements rather than their individual identities.

concepts.title: Texture Analysis and Synthesis Overview
concepts.one_liner: Texture analysis and synthesis serve as foundational problems for exploring image representations and precursors to modern deep learning approaches.
concepts.content: Texture analysis and synthesis are problems used to explore texture representations. These models are precursors of more modern approaches using deep learning. Many of the concepts and intuitions regarding why these models are successful are best understood by first exploring simple yet powerful statistical models.
concepts.motivation_md: Studying classical texture models provides the necessary intuition for how local patterns combine to form global structures, which is fundamental to understanding modern neural networks.
concepts.recap_md:
- Serves as a gateway to understanding complex image representations.
 - Provides foundational intuitions for modern deep learning methods.

 - Provides foundational intuitions for modern deep learning methods.

concepts.title: Infinite Texture Generation Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Texture synthesis can be solved by a trivial algorithm that crops pieces from a very large reference image to create new images.
concepts.content: Texture synthesis can be solved by a trivial algorithm as shown in (see figure: The infinite texture generation algorithm. If we had access to a very large image of the texture we want to generate, we could just crop pieces from it to create new images.). However, such an algorithm, although successful in practice, provides little understanding of how human perception works or how to modify textures to create new ones. Additionally, it does not help in identifying what representations can be useful to measure similarity between textures.
concepts.motivation_md: This trivial approach serves as a baseline for texture synthesis, highlighting the need for more sophisticated models that explain human perception and allow for texture manipulation.
concepts.recap_md: - Texture synthesis can be achieved by simply cropping pieces from a large reference image.

concepts.title: Intuition for Texture Perception

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Most observers perceive images with many similar elements as a single texture rather than a composition of individual, countable objects.
concepts.content: Most observers perceive an image of a stone wall, such as the one in [FIGURE:ecffb3dd8eb68d4d | A close-up photograph of a rustic stone wall composed of irregularly shaped, flat, and rounded stones of various sizes and earthy tones like grey, tan, and reddish-brown. The stones are tightly...], as a rock texture rather than a composition of countable rocks. While the rocks are indeed countable, doing so requires a significant effort, and most people do not care about the specific number of elements unless they are in the business of selling them.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why we treat complex visual scenes as textures, simplifying our visual processing by focusing on global patterns rather than individual components.
concepts.recap_md: - Observers naturally group numerous similar objects into a single texture representation.

concepts.title: Perception of Sets

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Human vision processes small groups of objects instantly but relies on linear counting or statistical set representation for larger groups.
concepts.content: When an image is composed of one or a few distinct objects, we can easily pay attention to each of them individually and count them in parallel. For displays with fewer than five elements, the time required to report the number does not depend on the count, as shown in (see figure: When looking at these images, we can count the number of circles at a glance if there are less than five circles. When an image has more than five items, we have to count them one by one.). However, when images are composed of more than five similarly looking elements, counting them requires looking at each one by one, and the time to count them grows linearly. In these cases, we seem to pay attention only to a few of them and represent the rest as a set.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how the brain transitions from individual object recognition to set-based perception is crucial for modeling how humans handle complex visual environments.
concepts.recap_md: - Humans can count up to four or five objects instantly through a process called subitizing.

concepts.title: Subitizing

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Subitizing is the ability to instantly determine the number of objects in a display without counting them, typically limited to fewer than five items.
concepts.content: The ability to know how many objects are in a display without counting them is called subitizing. This phenomenon only works when there are fewer than five elements in a display.
concepts.motivation_md: Subitizing represents a specialized, high-speed visual process for small quantities, distinct from the serial counting used for larger sets.
concepts.recap_md: - Subitizing allows for the near-instantaneous recognition of small quantities.

slots.motivation: Subitizing represents a specialized, high-speed visual process for small quantities, distinct from the serial counting used for larger sets.
slots.key_passage: - Subitizing allows for the near-instantaneous recognition of small quantities.

concepts.title: Visual Crowding

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Visual crowding is a phenomenon where objects in peripheral vision become difficult to recognize when surrounded by other similar features.
concepts.content: Crowding is a visual phenomenon where objects in the periphery become hard to identify when surrounded by other elements, as illustrated in (see figure: Crowding. If you look at the central cross, the letter R on the right can be recognized, however the letter B on the left is hard to read.). This occurs because the features of the target and its neighbors get entangled as if the pooling window for image features was larger than the items together. While fixating on a central point, it is easy to see that a peripheral region contains text, but it is hard to bind the features together to perceive individual letters. The circles in (see figure: Crowding. If you look at the central cross, the letter R on the right can be recognized, however the letter B on the left is hard to read.) represent an approximation of the size of the visual regions over which visual features are pooled.
concepts.motivation_md: Crowding demonstrates that peripheral vision relies on statistical representations of image features rather than high-resolution individual object recognition.
concepts.recap_md: - Crowding makes it difficult to distinguish individual objects in the periphery when they are closely spaced.

concepts.title: Textons

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Textons are fundamental texture elements, such as junctions and corners, whose statistical relationships define a texture's appearance.
concepts.content: Bela Julesz proposed that textures are analyzed in terms of statistical relationships between fundamental texture elements called textons. According to this model, textons might be represented by features such as the number of junctions, terminators, corners, and intersections within patterns. These models were often restricted to binary images formed by simple elements as shown in (see figure: Texture discrimination using textons.). While it is often easy to see the boundary between textures pre-attentively, the challenge is that detecting specific texton elements can be unreliable, making the representation non-robust.
concepts.motivation_md: Textons were an early attempt to define the "atoms" of texture, helping researchers understand how the human visual system discriminates between different patterns.
concepts.recap_md: - Textons are basic units like corners or terminators used to model texture perception.

concepts.title: Pre-Attentive Texture Discrimination

position.section_title: A Few Notes about Human Perception

concepts.one_liner: Pre-attentive texture discrimination is the ability to distinguish between different textures instantly and without conscious effort.
concepts.content: Pre-attentive texture discrimination refers to the ability to see boundaries between textures without making a conscious effort. Models based on filter banks, introduced by Bergen, Adelson, Malik, and Perona, demonstrated that filter outputs could explain several discrimination results. These features based on filter outputs can also be used for texture-based image segmentation.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept identifies the low-level visual processes that allow us to segment scenes into different regions based on texture automatically.
concepts.recap_md: - Pre-attentive discrimination occurs instantly without requiring focused attention.

concepts.title: The Problem of Texture Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: The problem of texture synthesis involves creating new random samples of a texture that match the statistical characteristics of a reference image.
concepts.content: The problem of texture synthesis involves building a process that, given a reference texture, outputs images with new random samples of the same texture. This is often achieved by transforming a reference texture into a representation using texture analysis (an encoder) to find parameters $\theta$. The synthesis procedure then takes a random noise image and these parameters to generate the desired output. Texture synthesis is important for computer graphics applications and for studying what representations of a texture are useful for visual recognition.
concepts.motivation_md: Texture synthesis allows for the generation of infinite variations of a pattern, which is useful for realistic rendering and testing theories of texture perception.
concepts.recap_md: - Texture synthesis aims to generate new images that are perceived as the same texture as a reference.

slots.motivation: Texture synthesis allows for the generation of infinite variations of a pattern, which is useful for realistic rendering and testing theories of texture perception.

concepts.title: Heeger-Bergen Texture Synthesis Method
concepts.one_liner: A wavelet-based texture synthesis method that matches histograms of filter responses across multiple orientations and scales to generate new images from noise.
concepts.content: The Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis method, published in 1995, is an influential wavelet-based algorithm for image synthesis. It is based on the conjecture that two textures appear identical to a human observer if they produce the same distribution of filter responses for all filters. The algorithm consists of two stages: texture analysis and texture synthesis. In the analysis stage, a reference texture is decomposed into multiple orientations and scales using a steerable pyramid, typically with six orientations and three scales. The final texture representation, $\theta$, is the concatenation of the 18 subband histograms, the low-pass residual histogram, and the input image histogram. (see figure: (a) Texture analysis (encoder) using a steerable pyramid with six orientations and three scales. The output representation is the concatenation of the 18 subband histograms, the low-pass residual...) The synthesis stage is an iterative procedure that begins with a random noise image and uses the parameters $\theta$ to produce a new improved image. (see figure: The steps of the Heeger-Bergen texture synthesis algorithm. The process starts with white noise input image. Each step takes as input the previous output, and it is modified by a function...) The crux of the algorithm is to alternate matching the intensity domain pixel histogram of the image and then matching the histograms of each subband in the transform domain. Histogram matching is implemented by a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity. (see figure: Histogram matching for one of the subbands. The same operation is done for all the subbands independently.) After several iterations, the algorithm converges to a synthesized texture. While effective for many textures, it may poorly depict large-scale structures as it does not capture correlations across scales. (see figure: Two examples of synthesized textures. Inputs have a size of 256 $\times$ 256 pixels, outputs are 512 $\times$ 512. In these examples, the algorithm runs for 15 iterations, using a pyramid of six...)
concepts.motivation_md: The method was developed to test the hypothesis that textures are perceptually identical if they share the same distribution of filter responses, providing a way to synthesize textures using multi-scale statistical matching.
concepts.recap_md: - Decomposes a reference texture into subbands using a steerable pyramid. - Iteratively matches histograms of the image and its filter subbands. - Represents texture as a concatenation of subband, low-pass residual, and image histograms.

concepts.title: Texture Analysis
concepts.one_liner: The process of extracting a texture representation, $\theta$, from a reference texture image.
concepts.content: Texture analysis of a reference texture extracts a texture representation, $\theta$. This representation captures the essential parameters or statistical properties of the reference image required to characterize its texture.
concepts.motivation_md: To create a compact mathematical or statistical description of a visual texture that can be used to generate new, similar samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Extracts a representation $\theta$ from a reference image. - Serves as the encoder stage in texture synthesis workflows.

slots.motivation: To create a compact mathematical or statistical description of a visual texture that can be used to generate new, similar samples.
slots.key_passage: - Extracts a representation $\theta$ from a reference image. - Serves as the encoder stage in texture synthesis workflows.
slots.example: Texture analysis of a reference texture extracts a texture representation, $\theta$. This representation captures the essential parameters or statistical properties of the reference image required to characterize its texture.

concepts.title: Texture Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: The procedure of using a texture representation, $\theta$, to generate new random samples that appear visually similar to the original texture.
concepts.content: Texture synthesis uses a representation, $\theta$, to generate new random samples of the same texture. In general, two textures are perceived as similar when they seem to be generated by the same physical process.
concepts.motivation_md: To generate large or infinite amounts of a specific texture from a small sample, which is useful in computer graphics and image editing.
concepts.recap_md: - Generates new samples based on a representation $\theta$. - Aims to produce images perceived as originating from the same process as the reference.

slots.motivation: To generate large or infinite amounts of a specific texture from a small sample, which is useful in computer graphics and image editing.
slots.key_passage: - Generates new samples based on a representation $\theta$. - Aims to produce images perceived as originating from the same process as the reference.
slots.example: Texture synthesis uses a representation, $\theta$, to generate new random samples of the same texture. In general, two textures are perceived as similar when they seem to be generated by the same physical process.

concepts.title: Histogram Matching for Texture Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: A technique that uses a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity to modify image or subband values so their distribution matches a target histogram.
concepts.content: Histogram matching is implemented by a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity. In texture synthesis, it is used to transform the subbands of a noise image to match the Laplacian-shaped histograms typical of natural textures. For example, the subband of input white noise has a Gaussian distribution; histogram matching modifies each subband pixel so the resulting subband looks sparser, with many values set to zero, matching the target reference. (see figure: Histogram matching for one of the subbands. The same operation is done for all the subbands independently.)
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a way to force the statistical distribution of a generated image to match the known statistics of a reference texture across different scales and orientations.
concepts.recap_md: - Employs a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity to adjust pixel value distributions. - Transforms Gaussian noise subbands to match the sparse distributions of natural textures.

slots.key_passage: - Employs a pointwise monotonic nonlinearity to adjust pixel value distributions. - Transforms Gaussian noise subbands to match the sparse distributions of natural textures.

concepts.title: Parametric Texture Models

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: Texture models that represent a texture using a fixed, low-dimensional set of statistical parameters.
concepts.content: Parametric texture models represent textures using a specific set of parameters, $\theta$, extracted during analysis. These models were the primary approach to texture synthesis until the emergence of nonparametric methods around the year 2000.
concepts.motivation_md: To provide a compact, efficient representation of texture that captures essential statistical properties without needing to store the entire original image.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses a low-dimensional representation $\theta$ to characterize textures. - Predominant in the field until the rise of nonparametric models.

concepts.title: Nonparametric Texture Models

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: Texture models that use the reference image itself as the representation, rather than a fixed set of parameters.
concepts.content: Nonparametric texture models became dominant after 2000, succeeding parametric models until the rise of neural generative models in 2014. In these models, the representation of a texture is typically the reference image itself. The advantage of this approach is that no information is lost in the representation.
concepts.motivation_md: To avoid the information loss inherent in low-dimensional parametric models and better capture complex, high-order spatial structures.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses the reference image itself as the texture representation. - Dominant between 2000 and the advent of deep learning generative models.

concepts.title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: A nonparametric texture synthesis model based on Markov random fields that generates pixels by sampling from similar neighborhoods in a reference image.
concepts.content: The Efros-Leung model is a nonparametric Markov random field image model where the probability distribution of a pixel is dependent on the neighborhood around it. In this model, the representation of a texture is the reference image itself, ensuring no information is lost. The synthesized texture changes as a function of the context region size: small regions may fail to capture complete structures, while larger regions enforce spatial regularities. concepts.title: Efros-Leung Algorithm

position.section_title: Efros-Leung Texture Analysis and Synthesis Model

concepts.one_liner: An iterative process that synthesizes texture by matching local neighborhoods in a reference image and copying corresponding pixel values.
concepts.content: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an iterative procedure for texture synthesis. At each iteration, the algorithm identifies the synthesized pixels in the neighborhood of the target pixel. It searches the input reference image for examples of similar pixel configurations, defined by a sum of squared intensity differences lower than a specific threshold. One of these matching instances is randomly selected, and its pixel value is copied to the synthesized image. This process is typically performed in a raster-scan ordering. Pixels without sufficient neighboring context can be randomly sampled from the input texture. (see figure: In the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99)
concepts.motivation_md: To provide a simple yet effective way to grow textures by mimicking the local conditional probability distributions found in a sample image.
concepts.recap_md: - Iteratively fills pixels based on local neighborhood similarity to the source. - Uses sum of squared differences (SSD) to find matching patches. - Can be implemented using a raster-scan ordering for synthesis.

slots.motivation: To provide a simple yet effective way to grow textures by mimicking the local conditional probability distributions found in a sample image.
slots.key_passage: - Iteratively fills pixels based on local neighborhood similarity to the source. - Uses sum of squared differences (SSD) to find matching patches. - Can be implemented using a raster-scan ordering for synthesis.

It searches the input reference image for examples of similar pixel configurations, defined by a sum of squared intensity differences lower than a specific threshold. One of these matching instances is randomly selected, and its pixel value is copied to the synthesized image. This process is typically performed in a raster-scan ordering. Pixels without sufficient neighboring context can be randomly sampled from the input texture. (see figure: In the Efros-Leung algorithm @Efros99)

concepts.title: Autoregressive Model Connection
concepts.one_liner: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an autoregressive model, a class of models that can be used in conjunction with deep networks for texture synthesis.
concepts.content: The Efros-Leung algorithm is an autoregressive model. This class of models can be used in conjunction with deep networks to generate textures and other data by modeling the probability of a pixel or element conditioned on previous ones.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models provide a structured way to generate complex data like textures by breaking the generation process into a sequence of conditional steps.
concepts.recap_md: - The Efros-Leung algorithm serves as a specific instance of an autoregressive model.

concepts.title: Diffusion Models Connection
concepts.one_liner: The iterative optimization of the Heeger-Bergen algorithm is a type of denoising process, similar to the strategy used in diffusion models.
concepts.content: The iterative optimization of the Heeger-Bergen algorithm is a type of denoising process: it starts with a noise image and little by little transforms it into an image of a texture. This general idea reappears in the context of diffusion models, which follow this same strategy.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the iterative refinement in early texture algorithms helps motivate the denoising strategies used in modern generative diffusion models.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) Connection
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and the Heeger-Bergen algorithm both aim to match the statistics of a generated image to those of exemplar images.
concepts.content: The Heeger-Bergen algorithm is connected to generative adversarial networks (GANs). The objective of Heeger-Bergen is to make a texture that has the same histogram statistics as an exemplar. Similarly, a GAN makes images that have the same statistics as a set of exemplars; however, the statistics we seek to match in a GAN are learned by a discriminator neural network rather than being hand-defined subband statistics.
concepts.motivation_md: This connection highlights the evolution from hand-crafted statistical matching to learned feature matching in generative modeling.
concepts.recap_md: - Both Heeger-Bergen and GANs seek to match the statistics of exemplar images.

prereq.rationale: The study of texture analysis and synthesis is predicated on the definition of texture as a statistical representation of constituent elements.
This algorithm is a specific technique for performing texture synthesis, which is the creation of new images based on texture properties.
Subitizing is the specific term for the parallel, instant counting process that occurs for small sets, as described in the broader study of set perception.
Textons are proposed as the fundamental primitives or 'atoms' that constitute a texture.
Julesz's theory of pre-attentive discrimination is based on the statistical distribution of these fundamental texture elements.
Pre-attentive discrimination is the mechanism that allows us to perceive textures as global entities without conscious inspection of individual parts.
Parametric models rely on a specific set of parameters extracted from a reference image during the analysis phase.
These models were historically the primary approach used for the task of texture synthesis.
The algorithm implements the nonparametric approach by searching the input reference image directly for similar pixel configurations.
The Efros-Leung algorithm is identified as a specific instance of an autoregressive model, which predicts elements based on previous ones.
The iterative optimization in Heeger-Bergen is framed as a denoising process, linking it to the strategy used in diffusion models.
Both GANs and Heeger-Bergen aim to match the statistics of a generated image to those of an exemplar.
Heeger-Bergen's use of histogram matching is the basis for its comparison with GAN-based statistical matching.
The problem of texture synthesis is defined in relation to the concept of texture as a set of statistical characteristics.
The algorithm relies on the psychophysical conjecture that matching filter response distributions is sufficient for human texture perception.
Texture analysis is the process of extracting the essential parameters that define a specific texture.
Texture analysis is defined as the first stage of the texture synthesis problem, where the reference image is encoded into parameters.
Texture synthesis requires the representation theta extracted during the analysis phase to generate new samples.
